article.headline: Four Dimensions, Zero Plugins: Gaussian Splatting Hits the Browser
article.lede: A clip circulating on X shows a photorealistic volumetric scene — a human figure in motion, captured simultaneously from a dome of cameras and rendered as a freely navigable world — playing back in real time inside an ordinary web browser. The interface labels “SCENE Fashion” and “ENVIRONMENT Street Dome” are consistent with 4DV.ai’s browser-native viewer, a Chinese platform built on PlayCanvas and the WebGPU rendering API that requires no download or install. Behind the impression of effortlessness lies a decade of compressive geometry research and two years of engineering to make GPU-side depth sorting viable in a consumer browser.
article.body:
The demo almost certainly originates from **4DV.ai**, whose PlayCanvas-based viewer streams *six-degrees-of-freedom* (6DoF) volumetric video to any modern browser. A dense array of cameras arranged in a dome captures the subject from every angle simultaneously; the footage is processed into a **4D Gaussian splat** — a cloud of millions of semi-transparent, time-varying ellipsoids — compressed to roughly 12.5 megabytes per second and served progressively. The result is a scene the viewer can orbit, approach, and walk through in real time, all rendered without a native application.

The foundation is **3D Gaussian Splatting** (3DGS), introduced by Kerbl et al. at SIGGRAPH 2023. Rather than tracing rays through a *neural radiance field* (NeRF) — a slow, memory-hungry neural network that dominated novel-view synthesis for three years — 3DGS represents a scene as millions of anisotropic ellipsoids, each carrying a position, size, opacity, and view-dependent colour encoded as *spherical harmonics*. A visibility-aware rasteriser projects and composites them in depth order every frame. Because there is no neural network in the render loop, the technique achieves over 100 frames per second on a desktop GPU.

Adding time to the representation — *4D Gaussian Splatting* — was formalised in two concurrent 2024 papers. Wu et al. (CVPR 2024) attach a lightweight *neural deformation field* to a canonical 3DGS scene: a small network predicts per-frame offsets for each Gaussian’s position, rotation, and scale, reaching 82 fps at 800×800 on an RTX 3090. Yang et al. (ICLR 2024) go further, constructing true four-dimensional Gaussian primitives with anisotropic covariance across both space and time simultaneously; their method introduces *4D spherindrical harmonics* to model appearance that varies with both viewpoint and moment in time. Both approaches were designed for CUDA-capable GPUs, which made browser deployment non-trivial.

The browser bottleneck is **depth sorting**. Correct *alpha compositing* of Gaussian splats requires ranking every primitive back-to-front relative to the camera every frame. Native runtimes do this with a GPU *radix sort* in microseconds. In a WebGL context — which lacks compute shaders — the sort falls to a CPU web worker and lags the render thread, producing visible popping artefacts during fast camera movement. *WebGPU*, now shipping across Chrome, Safari (iOS and macOS 26), and Firefox, provides the compute access needed for a full GPU-side sort. A 2026 paper on a renderer called WebSplatter devised a wait-free hierarchical sort that sidesteps the inter-workgroup atomic operations WebGPU initially lacked, achieving 1.2–4.5× speedups over naïve implementations and eliminating the artefacts on Apple M1 hardware entirely.

The fashion application is not coincidental. Gracia.ai, a startup that raised $1.7 million in late 2025, produced what it describes as the world’s first 4DGS runway show — for brand Karl Kani — letting viewers examine fabric texture and model movement from any angle in-browser. 4DV.ai’s professional capture system, **InfiniteStudio**, won Best in Show at SIGGRAPH 2025 Real-Time Live; it compresses 4D Gaussian streams to around 12.5 MB/s, playable on a Meta (META) Quest 3 headset or a laptop without installation. The compression milestone — the field has shrunk 4DGS scene sizes from roughly 100 gigabytes per minute to around one gigabyte over two years — is what made casual web streaming possible.

concepts.definition: A technique that represents a scene as millions of semi-transparent, anisotropic (non-spherical) ellipsoids, each with a position, size, opacity, and view-dependent colour. A fast rasteriser projects and blends them in depth order, achieving real-time rendering without any neural network in the render loop.

An extension of 3DGS that adds a time dimension, enabling reconstruction and real-time playback of dynamic scenes. Approaches vary: some attach a neural deformation field that warps a static Gaussian cloud each frame; others treat time as a fourth axis of a true four-dimensional primitive.

A method, dominant from 2020 to 2023, that encodes a 3D scene in the weights of a neural network. To render a view, rays are traced through the network at hundreds of sample points per pixel — accurate but orders of magnitude slower than Gaussian Splatting.

A filming technique using a large array of cameras arranged around a subject to record it from every angle simultaneously. The footage is processed into a 3D or 4D representation — such as a Gaussian splat or a mesh — that viewers can inspect from any vantage point.

The ability to move freely in all six ways a rigid body can move: translate left/right, up/down, forward/back, and rotate yaw/pitch/roll. A 6DoF viewer can physically walk around a captured scene, unlike 3DoF (rotation-only) 360-degree video.

A mathematical basis for representing how a function’s value changes across all directions from a point. In Gaussian Splatting, each ellipsoid stores its colour as spherical harmonic coefficients so the rendered hue shifts correctly with viewing angle, capturing glossy reflections and directional lighting.

A compact neural network that maps a time value and a Gaussian’s identity to a spatial displacement — translating, rotating, or scaling that ellipsoid for a specific frame. It allows a single set of Gaussians to animate across time without storing separate Gaussians per frame.

An extension of spherical harmonics to four dimensions (three spatial plus one temporal), introduced by Yang et al. at ICLR 2024 to model appearance that varies simultaneously with both the viewer’s direction and the moment in time. The name blends “spheri-” and “-cylindrical” basis functions.

A mathematical description of an ellipsoid’s shape: rather than expanding equally in all directions (isotropic, like a sphere), an anisotropic Gaussian can be elongated, flattened, or tilted along any axis. In 4DGS the covariance matrix spans both space and time, letting a single primitive represent a Gaussian that moves and deforms.

The process of ordering translucent primitives — here, Gaussian ellipsoids — from back to front relative to the camera before compositing them. Without correct depth order, closer splats blend incorrectly with farther ones, causing visual artefacts. In Gaussian Splatting this must happen every frame, making it the primary real-time bottleneck.

The technique of blending layers of partially transparent content using an opacity (alpha) channel. Gaussian Splatting uses an “over” compositing operator applied back-to-front: each ellipsoid contributes colour weighted by its opacity and the accumulated transparency of everything already composited in front of it.

A non-comparative sorting algorithm that processes integers digit by digit, achieving linear time complexity. On GPUs it is the standard approach for depth-sorting Gaussian splats because it exploits massive parallelism; implementing it correctly in WebGPU required workarounds for missing inter-workgroup atomic operations.

A modern browser graphics and compute API, successor to WebGL, that exposes compute shaders and general-purpose GPU programming to JavaScript. Unlike WebGL, it supports arbitrary parallel computation on the GPU rather than just graphics pipelines — the capability that enables proper GPU-side depth sorting for Gaussian Splatting in a browser.

ticker_meta.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
ticker_meta.blurb: Meta Platforms, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — collectively the largest social-media ecosystem in the world by monthly active users. The company generates the vast majority of its revenue through digital advertising, using detailed behavioural data to target ads across its platforms. After a painful 2022 in which shares fell roughly 65% amid a revenue slowdown and ballooning metaverse losses, Meta executed a dramatic turnaround by cutting costs, boosting margins, and rapidly integrating AI-driven ad ranking tools (Advantage+) that demonstrably improved advertiser returns. CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'Year of Efficiency' and the company followed through. By late 2025 Meta was simultaneously the most profitable it had ever been and the most aggressive in AI infrastructure spending, committing up to $65 billion in capex for 2025 and raising that figure to as much as $145 billion for 2026.
ticker_meta.recent: Meta reached an all-time high near $796 per share in September 2025. The stock declined approximately 24–28% from that peak through April 2026, with the primary investor concern being the scale of the 2026 capital-expenditure commitment — up to $145 billion — and uncertainty about whether AI-driven revenue would materialise at the pace required to justify it. Quarterly earnings remained strong through the period, but multiple compression drove share-price weakness.
